paras: The attempted lynching of L. W. Davis took place at Winslow, Arizona Territory, on July 4, 1888, when railroad firemen and engineers tried to hang the roundhouse night watchman for fatally shooting a fireman. The men put a rope around his neck but dispersed after two engineers urged them to let the law take its course, and Davis was jailed at St. Johns on a murder charge. The story spread as a one-line wire item noting that the "murderer narrowly escaped lynching by a mob."

Davis, an old man, worked as night watchman at the Atlantic & Pacific railroad roundhouse in Winslow. According to the Albuquerque wire, the fireman "had a few words" with him "about some oil"; territorial papers said the quarrel was over supplies. The Florence Arizona Weekly Enterprise said the argument became a fist fight in which the watchman was "worsted," after which he left to get a gun.
Meeting the fireman again, he opened fire, and two bullets struck him. The wire said the fireman died in ten minutes, while the Enterprise said he lived a few hours.

The firemen and engineers then "organized a vigilance committee for the purpose of hanging the murderer" and went so far as to place a rope around his neck. Two engineers who were "cooler than the balance of their comrades" addressed the crowd and urged it to give the man "a chance for life." After long discussion the mob dispersed, and the watchman was taken to St. Johns, the county seat, for safekeeping.

A coroner's jury found that Davis had killed Reinhold Schneider "criminally, unlawfully and with malice aforethought." The St. Johns Herald later reported that Constable McKinney had brought Davis up from Winslow and lodged him in jail on a murder charge. The paper predicted that Davis, "if he escapes hanging," would likely receive a long prison term, but no report of an indictment or trial was found.

The first report to reach distant readers was an Albuquerque dispatch of July 6, printed in the Los Angeles Daily Herald's "Coast Cullings" column on July 7 and in the Tucson Arizona Weekly Citizen a week later. It named only "a fireman named Snyder," called the watchman "the murderer," and treated the near-lynching in a single clause. When the brief reached news digests in Oregon and Idaho later in July, even that clause had been cut, leaving only the shooting.

Arizona papers carried fuller items, the Prescott Journal-Miner and the Mohave County Miner in their "Territorial Items" columns and the Florence Enterprise under the headline "Murder at Winslow." The Enterprise described the mob without censure but credited "wiser counsel" for its dispersal. The St. Johns Herald, published where Davis was jailed, reported the inquest and the charge but did not mention the mob.

The papers disagree on names and date. The Journal-Miner and the Enterprise called the men Snyder and Davidson, while the St. Johns Herald and the Mohave County Miner gave Reinhold Schneider and L. W. Davis. Four Arizona papers, including the St. Johns Herald that reported the inquest, dated the shooting July 4, but the Albuquerque wire placed it on the evening of July 5. The St. Johns Herald also gave the time as afternoon rather than evening.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of L. W. Davis at Winslow
bases: Railroad firemen and engineers formed a 'vigilance committee' to hang the accused killer and put a rope around his neck before being talked out of it, an attempted lynching with no one killed by the mob (A5, A1, A2, A6).

A mob of firemen and engineers acting without legal authority set out to hang Davis for the killing of Schneider, but dispersed after two engineers urged them to let the law take its course, so no one was killed by the group (A5, A1, A6). The only death was the shooting of the fireman by the watchman himself (A3).

The wire brief (A1, A4) and three separate territorial items (A2, A5, A6) agree that the watchman narrowly escaped lynching after the shooting, though only A5 gives details of the mob and the St. Johns Herald (A3, A7) does not mention it.

accounts.label: Wire report (Albuquerque, July 6)
accounts.gist: A fireman named Snyder had words with the night watchman about oil and was shot twice, dying in ten minutes; the 'murderer narrowly escaped lynching by a mob' and was taken to St. Johns.

accounts.label: Arizona Weekly Enterprise
accounts.gist: A dispute over supplies became a fist fight; Davidson, worsted, got a gun and shot Snyder, who died hours later; firemen and engineers put a rope around his neck before two engineers talked them down.

accounts.label: St. Johns Herald / coroner's jury
accounts.gist: L. W. Davis shot and killed Reinhold Schneider on the afternoon of the 4th; the coroner's jury found malice aforethought, and Davis was jailed for murder.

framing.detail: Coast and territorial papers ran the Albuquerque brief, calling the watchman 'the murderer'; later Oregon and Idaho digests cut it to the shooting alone.
The Florence 'Murder at Winslow' item described the mob without condemning it but credited the 'cooler' engineers and 'wiser counsel' with saving 'the man a chance for life'.
The St. Johns Herald reported the inquest and jailing, omitted the mob, and predicted Davis would hang or go to prison.
